title: Panic, handmaid of fear (phuza)
greek: φύζα (phuza), φόβου κρυόεντος ἑταίρη (phobou kruoentos hetairē)
short: Murray's 'Panic' is phuza, literally 'flight'; Homer personifies it as the companion of chilling Fear (Phobos).
body: The Greek says that a 'god-sent phuza, companion of chilling phobos' held the Achaeans. Both nouns come from words for running away: phuza is related to pheugō, 'flee', and phobos in Homer usually means 'rout' rather than inward fear. Walter Leaf notes that phuza has here already moved from the act of flight towards the emotion of terror, the sense that phobos later took over completely. The adjective kruoeis, 'chilling, freezing' (Murray's 'numbing'), makes fear a physical cold. The personification matters: as in Book 4, where Terror and Rout attend Ares, the emotions of battle are imagined as divine agents that seize men from outside. The book opens with the Achaeans at their lowest point after the Trojan victory of Book 8, the situation that makes the embassy to Achilles necessary. Gregory Nagy adds that hetairē is a verse-final form, an analogically levelled replacement for older hetaira, found only here in the Iliad.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.2

title: Simile of the two winds from Thrace
greek: Βορέης καὶ Ζέφυρος, τώ τε Θρῄκηθεν ἄητον (Boreēs kai Zephyros, tō te Thrēikēthen aēton)
short: The Achaeans' divided hearts are compared to a sea whipped up by the North and West Winds blowing together out of Thrace.
body: The simile pictures a sudden squall in which two winds strike the sea at once, raise a dark wave and throw seaweed up on the beach; 'even so' the Achaeans' hearts are torn. Leaf takes the two winds as the image of conflicting fears pulling the army two ways. He also notes that the description implies a poet looking at the sea from the coast of Asia Minor or a nearby island: from there both Boreas (north) and Zephyrus (west) can be said to come 'from Thrace', and the weed is driven up on the speaker's own shore. Nagy observes that the passage moves in a ring from the grief of the whole army to the grief in Agamemnon's own heart (9.8-9). Storm and sea similes recur at the great crises of the battle for the ships (compare 11.305-8 and 15.624-8).

title: Agamemnon weeping like a dark spring
greek: κρήνη μελάνυδρος (krēnē melanudros), αἰγίλιψ πέτρη (aigilips petrē)
short: Agamemnon weeps like a dark-watered spring trickling down a sheer rock face; the same simile is used of Patroclus weeping in Book 16.
body: The king who will offer the embassy stands before the assembly in tears 'like a spring of dark water that pours its dusky stream down a sheer cliff'. Leaf explains the picture as the thin but unceasing trickle of a spring that emerges on a cliff face and stains it with dark streaks, a common sight in limestone country, rather than a deep well. The rare adjective aigilips (Murray's 'beetling') is of unknown derivation; the ancient explanation was 'so steep that even goats leave it'. The ancient editor Zenodotus omitted the simile, and Leaf thought it borrowed from 16.3-4, where Patroclus comes weeping to Achilles in the same words. The echo is meaningful whichever passage came first: both men weep for the Achaean losses, and both tears lead to appeals to Achilles, the first refused, the second granted with fatal results.

title: Sceptre without valour: Diomedes' rebuke
greek: διάνδιχα (diandicha); σκήπτρῳ μέν τοι δῶκε τετιμῆσθαι ... ἀλκὴν δ' οὔ τοι δῶκεν
short: Diomedes tells Agamemnon that Zeus gave him only half a gift: the sceptre and its honour, but not the valour that is the greatest power.
body: Diomedes answers Agamemnon's call to flee by turning the king's own earlier insult back on him: in Book 4 (4.370-400) Agamemnon had taunted him as unworthy of his father Tydeus, and Diomedes then kept silent out of respect. Now he speaks 'where it is right, in the assembly'. Zeus, he says, endowed Agamemnon diandicha, 'by halves' in Leaf's rendering: with the sceptre, that is, honour and rank (timē), but not with alkē, the fighting courage that is 'the greatest might'. The phrase restates the central problem of the Iliad: the king who holds authority is not the best warrior. Nestor made the same distinction between Agamemnon and Achilles in the quarrel of Book 1 (1.277-81), and Achilles will turn it into an argument against the whole system of honour later in this book. Diomedes' defiant 'Sthenelus and I will fight on' (9.48-9) shows the courage the king lacks.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.37

title: Clanless, lawless, hearthless
greek: ἀφρήτωρ ἀθέμιστος ἀνέστιος (aphrētōr athemistos anestios)
short: Nestor's three-word curse on the lover of civil strife: a man outside the phratry, outside customary law (themis), and without a hearth.
body: Each adjective negates one bond of early Greek society. Aphrētōr denies membership of a phrētrē, the brotherhood or clan group (compare Nestor's advice to marshal the army 'by phratries' at 2.362-3); athemistos denies a share in themis, the body of traditional right administered by kings; anestios denies a hearth (hestia), the centre of household worship. Leaf glosses the couplet as banishment from tribe, law and home, and notes that the lines are quoted in Aristophanes (Peace 1097) and were expanded by Cicero (Philippics 13.1). He also remarks that the lines sit a little awkwardly here, since Nestor's real proposal, the reparation to Achilles, is postponed until later in the scene. The words cast a shadow forward: Achilles, who withdraws from the common enterprise, will describe himself as treated like an outcast without rights (9.648).

title: Atē: Agamemnon's 'blindness'
greek: ἀασάμην, οὐδ' αὐτὸς ἀναίνομαι (aasamēn, oud' autos anainomai); ἄτη (atē)
short: Agamemnon admits that he acted in atē, a god-sent derangement of judgement, and offers compensation; atē will reappear as a goddess in Phoenix's allegory.
body: Murray's 'blind' and 'blind folly' translate the verb aaomai and the noun atē, a state of mental confusion that leads to a ruinous act. At the start of the book Agamemnon blamed Zeus for binding him in atē (9.18, repeating 2.111); here, before the council, he concedes 'I was deluded, I do not deny it myself', and so offers apoina, compensation. E. R. Dodds made this concept the starting point of The Greeks and the Irrational: Homeric men attribute rash acts to an outside power without thereby escaping the duty to pay for them. Agamemnon's fullest 'apology', in Book 19 (19.86-138), blames Zeus, Moira and the Erinys and tells the story of Atē herself, eldest daughter of Zeus. Nagy translates atē here as 'aberration' and, in a separate comment on 9.158-161, notes that the offer still ends by reasserting Agamemnon's superiority, which undercuts the apology. Phoenix's allegory of the Prayers (9.502-12) turns atē against Achilles: whoever rejects an apology may be struck by atē in turn.

title: Agamemnon's gifts (apoina)
greek: ἀπερείσι' ἄποινα (apereisi' apoina)
short: Agamemnon offers 'boundless compensation': tripods, gold, horses, women, his daughter and seven cities. Scholars debate whether the gifts honour Achilles or subordinate him.
body: Apoina is the word used for the ransom Chryses offers for his daughter in Book 1 (1.13) and Priam's ransom for Hector in Book 24; here it means compensation for an insult. The list is enormous: seven untouched tripods, ten talents of gold, twenty cauldrons, twelve prize-winning horses, seven women of Lesbos and Briseis herself (with an oath that he has not slept with her), a share of the sack of Troy, one of his daughters without bride-price, and seven cities. Leaf observes that the value of a talent of gold seems modest (at 23.269 two talents rank below a cauldron). Walter Donlan argued that an ancient audience would hear such a gift as a move in a contest of status: by giving more than can ever be returned, Agamemnon makes Achilles his dependent, and the offer ends by demanding that Achilles 'submit' to the more kingly man. Nagy likewise stresses that the offer closes with Agamemnon's claim of superiority, which Odysseus prudently leaves out.

sources.cite: Walter Donlan, 'Duelling with Gifts in the Iliad: As the Audience Saw It', Colby Quarterly 29.3 (1993)

title: Agamemnon's three daughters
greek: Χρυσόθεμις καὶ Λαοδίκη καὶ Ἰφιάνασσα (Chrysothemis, Laodikē, Iphianassa)
short: Homer names three living daughters and never mentions the sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis; later poets either equated Iphianassa with Iphigenia or kept them apart.
body: The list is famous for what it leaves out. In the Iliad there is no sacrifice of Iphigenia: the story that Agamemnon killed his daughter to win a wind for Troy belongs to the Cypria and to tragedy. Leaf notes that Iphianassa here may originally be the same figure as Iphigenia, but that according to the Cypria Agamemnon had four daughters, Iphigenia and Iphianassa being distinct; Sophocles follows this when his Electra speaks of Chrysothemis and Iphianassa as still alive (Electra 157-8). Laodice was identified with Electra by Stesichorus and Xanthus (Leaf, citing Jebb). Lucretius, conversely, calls the sacrificed girl 'Iphianassa' (1.85). Orestes, named just before (9.142), is mentioned in the Iliad only in this offer and Odysseus' repetition of it. For a student reading Aeschylus' Oresteia alongside Homer, this line is a reminder that the epic knows Agamemnon as a father of living daughters offering one of them as a bride.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.143-145

title: Without bride-price (anaednon)
greek: ἀνάεδνον (anaednon); ἕδνα (hedna), μείλια (meilia)
short: Achilles may take a daughter without paying the hedna, the bride-gifts a suitor normally gave; Agamemnon will even add a dowry (meilia).
body: In the Homeric world a suitor usually won a bride by giving hedna, gifts to her father; Leaf states that the original and dominant meaning of the word in Homer is bride-price. The bride's father might in turn send her with gifts of his own, here called meilia, 'soothing gifts', which Murray renders as 'dower'. Agamemnon waives the first and promises the second on an unheard-of scale, 'such as no man ever yet gave with his daughter'. M. I. Finley used passages like this to show how marriage in Homer worked through an exchange of gifts between households rather than a simple purchase. The offer is generous but also binding: as Agamemnon's son-in-law, 'honoured like Orestes', Achilles would become a member of Agamemnon's household and therefore his subordinate. Achilles' reply (9.388-400) refuses the marriage pointedly: Peleus will find him a wife at home.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.146

title: The seven cities near Pylos
greek: ἑπτὰ ... εὖ ναιόμενα πτολίεθρα (hepta eu naiomena ptoliethra)
short: Agamemnon offers seven coastal towns on the border of 'sandy Pylos' in Messenia; Strabo tried to identify them and argued they must have belonged to the Atreidae.
body: The towns are Cardamyle, Enope, Hire, Pherae, Antheia, Aepeia and Pedasus, 'all near the sea, on the furthest border of sandy Pylos'. The geographer Strabo discusses them at length (8.4.1-5). He reasons that Agamemnon would not have promised cities that belonged neither to himself nor to his brother Menelaus, so Messenia must once have been under Atreid control. He identifies Pedasus with Methone (8.4.3), places Pherae and Cardamyle on the Messenian Gulf, and records rival views about the others: Enope was variously Pellana, a place near Cardamyle, or Gerenia; Aepeia was said to be Thuria, or alternatively Methone. Several sites are still uncertain. More important than the map is the political meaning: the inhabitants will honour Achilles 'like a god' and pay him dues, but they lie inside Agamemnon's sphere, so the gift would make Achilles a vassal lord under the Atreid king, as Donlan argues.

sources.cite: Strabo, Geography 8.4.1, 8.4.3-5 (trans. H. L. Jones, Loeb, 1927)
Walter Donlan, 'Duelling with Gifts in the Iliad: As the Audience Saw It', Colby Quarterly 29.3 (1993)

title: 'More kingly': the sting in Agamemnon's offer
greek: βασιλεύτερος (basileuteros); Ἀΐδης ... ἀμείλιχος ἠδ' ἀδάμαστος (Aidēs ameilichos ēd' adamastos)
short: Agamemnon ends his offer by demanding that Achilles yield, like the unbending Hades, to the 'more kingly' and older man; Odysseus omits these lines when he speaks.
body: Agamemnon's speech closes not with reconciliation but with a demand: 'let him yield; Hades is implacable and unconquerable, and so most hateful of gods to mortals; let him submit to me, since I am more kingly and older'. Hades, who accepts no gifts or pleas, is the image of the unbending man. The comparative basileuteros, 'more kingly', was also Agamemnon's claim in the quarrel of Book 1. When Odysseus repeats the list of gifts to Achilles almost word for word (9.264-99), he silently drops these lines and substitutes an appeal to pity the other Achaeans and to win glory by killing Hector. Nagy discusses both the claim of superiority and its omission. The phrase returns with irony in Book 10, where Agamemnon tells Diomedes not to let respect for rank decide his choice of companion, 'not even if he is more kingly' (10.239), while the narrator says he feared for his brother Menelaus. Achilles' opening reply, hating the man who 'hides one thing in his mind and says another', may answer what Odysseus left unsaid.

title: Phoenix
greek: Φοῖνιξ (Phoinix)
short: Achilles' old tutor appears suddenly in Agamemnon's council; Nestor names him first of the envoys, and many scholars think he was added to an older two-man embassy.
body: Phoenix, son of Amyntor, was given a refuge and a kingdom over the Dolopians by Peleus, and helped to raise the infant Achilles (his own story at 9.447-95). Leaf considers him evidently a late-comer to the story: he is introduced abruptly, there is no explanation of why he is in Agamemnon's council rather than with Achilles, and he is ignored from 9.168 to 9.432 apart from Ajax's nod at 9.223. Nestor sets the order Phoenix, Ajax, Odysseus and reinforces it with glances, yet Odysseus speaks first without introduction (Nagy). Whether Phoenix belongs to an expansion of the story or not, he is now central: his speech (9.434-605) is the longest in the Iliad, combining personal memories, the allegory of the Prayers and the story of Meleager, and he is the one envoy Achilles invites to stay. The name Phoinix ('Phoenician', 'purple-red', also the date-palm) has no clear connection with his role.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.168

anchor: So the twain went their way
title: The problem of the duals
greek: τὼ δὲ βάτην (tō de batēn) and other dual forms
short: Three envoys and two heralds go to Achilles, yet the Greek repeatedly uses dual forms ('the two of them'). Who are the two? The question has been argued since antiquity.
body: Greek has a dual number for exactly two persons, and in 9.182-98 the envoys are described with dual verbs, pronouns and participles: Murray's 'the twain'. But Nestor sent Phoenix, Ajax and Odysseus. Leaf summarises the ancient answers: Zenodotus held that the dual could stand for the plural; Aristarchus suggested that Phoenix had been sent on ahead, so that only two arrived together. Leaf himself rejects both ancient answers and concludes that Phoenix's speech was taken from another context and fitted into an original story of two envoys, Ajax and Odysseus, which is the analytic solution to the problem. Others look for meaning in the text as it stands: Charles Segal (1968) and Gregory Nagy suggest that the referents shift as Odysseus takes the lead, and Nagy reads Achilles' dual greeting (9.197-8), 'you two, dearest of the Achaeans', as pointedly excluding Odysseus, whom Achilles soon treats as an adversary. No single explanation has won general agreement, which makes the passage a good test case for the oral and analytic approaches to Homer.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.168
Charles Segal, 'The Embassy and the Duals of Iliad 9.182-98', Greek, Roman and Byzantine Studies 9 (1968) 101-114
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.182-198 and I.09.193-198

title: Achilles sings the klea andrōn
greek: ἄειδε δ' ἄρα κλέα ἀνδρῶν (aeide d' ara klea andrōn)
short: The envoys find Achilles singing 'the glorious deeds of men' to a lyre taken from Eëtion's city: the hero who has withdrawn from war performs epic poetry himself.
body: Klea andrōn, 'the famous deeds of men', is the Homeric phrase for heroic song itself; the bard Demodocus sings klea andrōn in Odyssey 8.73. Leaf notes that this is the only scene in the Iliad of music-making among men (the other concert, 1.603-4, is among the gods) and that the lyre's silver cross-bar marks it as rich booty; it comes from the sack of Thebe, the city of Andromache's father Eëtion. The scene is full of irony: Achilles, who is refusing to win kleos, sings of the kleos of others, and he will soon declare that he must choose between 'imperishable kleos' and a long life (9.413). Patroclus sits silent, 'waiting until Achilles should cease from singing'. Nagy interprets this as a picture of relay performance, one singer taking up the song where the other stops, as rhapsodes did, and notes that Patroclus' own name means 'he who has the kleos of the ancestors'.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.186-188
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.185-191

title: Achilles as host
greek: μείζονα δὴ κρητῆρα ... ζωρότερον δὲ κέραιε (meizona dē krētēra ... zōroteron de keraie)
short: Even in his anger Achilles receives the envoys with full guest-friendship: a larger mixing-bowl, stronger wine, a carved meal and an offering to the gods.
body: The scene is a model of Homeric hospitality (xenia): the guests are greeted, seated on purple rugs, given wine and meat before any business is discussed, and the gods receive their share when Patroclus throws the first portions into the fire (9.219-20). Achilles carves the meat himself, an honour to his guests. The order to mix the wine zōroteron has been debated since antiquity. Aristotle (Poetics 25) argued that it did not mean 'less watered', as for drunkards, but 'more quickly'; Leaf answers that ordinary Greek usage supports 'stronger', i.e. less diluted, as in Herodotus 6.84. Odysseus' first words exploit the setting: 'of the equal feast we have no lack', both here and in Agamemnon's hut (9.225-8). The courtesy of the meal contrasts sharply with the hardness of Achilles' answer, and the scene of eating together looks forward to the meal Achilles shares with Priam in Book 24.

sources.cite: Aristotle, Poetics 25, 1461a (on zōroteron)

title: Peleus' advice: philophrosunē
greek: φιλοφροσύνη γὰρ ἀμείνων (philophrosunē gar ameinōn)
short: Odysseus quotes Peleus' parting advice to his son: curb your proud spirit, for friendliness of mind is better, and keep away from strife.
body: Philophrosunē, 'kindliness, friendly-mindedness', is a rare word, and Odysseus uses the father's voice to give it authority: Peleus told Achilles that strength is the gift of Athena and Hera, but restraint of the great-hearted spirit (thumos) is his own task. The quotation is pointed because the quarrel in Book 1 was exactly a failure to hold back thumos. Leaf notes that in Book 11 Nestor quotes a quite different charge of Peleus, given on the same occasion when Odysseus and Nestor came to recruit Achilles: 'always to be best and to excel over others' (11.784), the line that sums up heroic ambition. The two remembered sayings show how a father's words can be shaped to the speaker's purpose. Phoenix will return to the same theme, telling Achilles to 'master his great spirit' because even the gods can bend (9.496-7).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.253
Homer, Iliad 11.783-4 (Peleus' other charge to Achilles)
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed., s.v. φιλοφροσύνη

anchor: even as the gates of Hades
title: Hateful as the gates of Hades
greek: ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσιν (echthros gar moi keinos homōs Aidao pulēisin)
short: Achilles hates, like the gates of death, the man who hides one thing in his mind and says another: plain speaking aimed at Odysseus.
body: Achilles says he must speak 'outright' (apēlegeōs, 'without regard', in Leaf's explanation) so that the envoys do not sit and 'coo' at him from either side. Then he states a principle: hateful to him as Hades' gates is the man who conceals one thing and says another. The words fit Odysseus, the master of cunning who has just edited Agamemnon's message, and Nagy reads them as marking enmity between the two heroes. In the Odyssey the same couplet is spoken by Odysseus himself, disguised as a beggar, when he swears to Eumaeus that he tells the truth (Od. 14.156-7), an irony that Homer's audience may have enjoyed. Adam Parry's influential essay 'The Language of Achilles' argued that in this speech Achilles strains the shared heroic vocabulary to say something it was not made to say: that the honour he fought for is empty.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.309-311
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.312-313
Homer, Odyssey 14.156-7 (the same lines in Odysseus' mouth)
Adam Parry, 'The Language of Achilles', Transactions and Proceedings of the American Philological Association 87 (1956) 1-7

title: Equal shares for coward and brave
greek: ἴση μοῖρα μένοντι ... ἐν δὲ ἰῇ τιμῇ ἠμὲν κακὸς ἠδὲ καὶ ἐσθλός (isē moira menonti ... en de iēi timēi)
short: Achilles attacks the system of honour itself: the man who stays behind gets the same share (moira), coward and brave the same honour (timē), and both die alike.
body: Moira here keeps its basic sense of 'share, portion', the part of the spoils assigned to each fighter, before it means 'fate'. In the heroic economy a warrior's timē, his honour, is made visible in such shares and in prizes such as Briseis. Achilles claims that this exchange has broken down: Agamemnon 'stays behind' by the ships and keeps the most (9.330-3), so that risking one's life buys nothing. The final line, 'the idle man and the one who has done much both die alike', moves from a complaint about Agamemnon to a reflection on mortality that leads to his choice of fates (9.410-16). Adam Parry and later critics see here the moment when Achilles questions the values of the Iliad from within; Donlan reads the speech as a refusal to accept the dependency that Agamemnon's gifts would create.

sources.cite: Adam Parry, 'The Language of Achilles', TAPA 87 (1956) 1-7
Walter Donlan, 'Duelling with Gifts in the Iliad: As the Audience Saw It', Colby Quarterly 29.3 (1993)
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed., s.v. μοῖρα

title: Simile of the mother bird
greek: ὡς δ' ὄρνις ἀπτῆσι νεοσσοῖσι προφέρῃσι μάστακ' (hōs d' ornis aptēsi neossoisi propherēisi mastak')
short: Achilles compares himself to a bird that brings every morsel to her unfledged chicks while faring badly herself: the warrior as provider for an ungrateful army.
body: It is striking that the greatest warrior chooses a maternal, almost domestic image for himself. The bird carries food 'in her bill' (mastax; Leaf discusses whether the word means 'mouth' or 'morsel' and prefers 'in her bill') and gives all to the nestlings, 'but with herself it goes badly'. Achilles applies it to his sleepless nights and bloody days, fought 'for the sake of their women', that is, for Menelaus' Helen. The simile sharpens his grievance: the giver receives nothing back. Homer uses similar tender imagery of Achilles elsewhere: in Book 16 Achilles compares the weeping Patroclus to a little girl tugging at her mother's dress (16.7-10). Leaf also notes the characteristic final touch of the simile, the bird's own hardship, which is exactly the point of comparison.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.324
Homer, Iliad 16.7-10 (Achilles' simile of the little girl)

title: Achilles' raids in the Troad
greek: δώδεκα ... πόλεις ... πεζὸς δ' ἕνδεκα (dōdeka poleis ... pezos d' hendeka)
short: Before the Iliad begins Achilles has sacked twelve cities by sea and eleven by land around Troy; his war-prizes, Briseis among them, come from these raids.
body: The Iliad presupposes nine years of raiding on the coasts and islands near Troy, in which Achilles was the chief sacker of cities. Leaf lists the towns named in the poem as taken by him: Thebe (1.366), Lyrnessus (2.691, 19.296), Pedasus (20.92), Tenedos (11.625), Lesbos (9.129) and Scyros (9.668). Briseis was taken at Lyrnessus; the lyre Achilles plays comes from Thebe; the seven women of Lesbos offered by Agamemnon were chosen from Achilles' own capture. Achilles' complaint is that he handed all the spoil to Agamemnon, who 'staying behind by the ships' distributed little and kept most. Nagy suggests that the eleven cities taken on foot may allude to the twelve cities of the Aeolian Dodecapolis (less Smyrna), so that Achilles' conquests serve as a charter myth for the Aeolian settlement of the region.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.329
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.328-333
Homer, Iliad 1.366-9 (the sack of Thebe)

title: Briseis: 'my wife', 'won by my spear'
greek: ἄλοχον θυμαρέα (alochon thumarea); δουρικτητήν περ ἐοῦσαν (douriktētēn per eousan)
short: Achilles calls Briseis his 'wife, dear to my heart', loved though 'spear-won'; comparing her with Helen, he exposes the war's own cause.
body: In Book 1 Briseis was Achilles' geras, the prize of honour. Here he uses the word for a wedded wife (alochos) and turns the logic of the war against the Atreidae: 'Are the sons of Atreus the only men who love their wives? Any decent and sensible man loves and cares for his own, as I loved her with all my heart, though she was won by my spear.' Douriktētos, 'acquired with the spear', is the term for a captive. Nagy stresses the irony of Achilles questioning why the Achaeans must fight for Helen. The speech should be read with Briseis' own lament for Patroclus (19.282-300), where she recalls that Patroclus promised to make her Achilles' wedded wife in Phthia. Whether Achilles' love is real or rhetorical is debated; the poem does not let the captive woman speak for herself until Book 19.

sources.cite: Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.340-343
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed., s.v. δουρίκτητος
Homer, Iliad 19.295-300 (Briseis' lament: Patroclus' promise)

title: 'Dog-faced': a Homeric insult
greek: κύνεός περ ἐών (kuneos per eōn)
short: Agamemnon, 'shameless as he is, dog-like though he be', would not dare to look Achilles in the face: the dog is Homer's image of shamelessness.
body: Literally the Greek says 'though he is dog-like'. Leaf refers back to Achilles' insult in the quarrel of Book 1, 'you with the eyes of a dog' (1.225), and to Zeus' words to Hera at the end of Book 8, that nothing is more dog-like than she; in Book 21 the gods even call each other 'dog-fly' (kunamuia, 21.394, 421). In Homeric culture the dog stands for lack of aidōs, the sense of shame that should restrain a person; it eats carrion and fawns or snaps without discrimination. Helen calls herself 'dog-faced' in self-reproach (3.180, 6.344). Margaret Graver's study of 'dog-Helen' argues that the insult names a specific failing, the shameless pursuit of one's own appetite, rather than a general obscenity. Here it confirms Achilles' charge that Agamemnon is 'clothed in shamelessness' (9.372) and so cannot be trusted with any further gifts or promises.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.373

title: Orchomenus and hundred-gated Egyptian Thebes
greek: Ὀρχομενός (Orchomenos); Θῆβαι Αἰγύπτιαι ... ἑκατόμπυλοι (Thēbai Aiguptiai ... hekatompuloi)
short: Achilles would refuse even the wealth of Minyan Orchomenus or of Egyptian Thebes with its hundred gates; the lines are the only mention of Egypt's Thebes in Homer.
body: Achilles names the two proverbially rich cities of his world. Orchomenus in Boeotia was the city of the Minyans, famous for treasure; Leaf points to Pausanias, who describes the great 'Treasury of Minyas' there (9.38.2), in fact a Mycenaean tholos tomb. Thebes in Upper Egypt (Luxor), seat of the Egyptian kings, is named in the Iliad only here, with its 'hundred gates' each sending out two hundred men with chariots; the Odyssey also knows the wealth of Egyptian Thebes (Od. 4.126-7). Leaf argues that 9.382-4 are a prosy interpolation, partly borrowed from the Odyssey, since Egypt is otherwise unknown to the Iliad and the pairing with Orchomenus points to Boeotian Thebes; he adds that almost all critics since Heyne have condemned 383-4. Not every modern reader agrees. Either way, the lines make the rhetorical point: no conceivable sum of gifts, 'not if they were as many as sand and dust', will buy Achilles back.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.381-384

title: The psychē that passes the barrier of the teeth
greek: ἀνδρὸς δὲ ψυχὴ πάλιν ἐλθεῖν οὔτε λεϊστὴ οὔθ' ἑλετή, ἐπεὶ ἄρ κεν ἀμείψεται ἕρκος ὀδόντων
short: Cattle and tripods can be raided or bought, but a man's psychē, once it has passed 'the fence of his teeth', cannot be taken back by raid or by purchase.
body: This is the philosophical centre of Achilles' reply. Leaf distinguishes the two ways of acquiring wealth: lēistos, 'to be won by raiding', and ktētos or helētos, 'to be gained' by trade or gift. The psychē, Murray's 'spirit', is in Homer the breath-soul that leaves the body through the mouth or a wound at death and goes as a shade to Hades; it is not yet the moral 'soul' of Plato. Jan Bremmer's study describes it as the 'free soul' that has no role in a living man's thinking but represents his life as a whole. The phrase 'fence of the teeth' (herkos odontōn) normally appears in the formula 'what word has escaped the fence of your teeth' (as at 4.350); Leaf notes that its use with the departing psychē is found only here. The contrast between replaceable goods and an irreplaceable life overturns the heroic exchange of risk for prizes.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.406-409
Jan Bremmer, The Early Greek Concept of the Soul, Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1983
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed., s.v. ψυχή

title: The choice of Achilles: two kēres
greek: διχθαδίας κῆρας φερέμεν θανάτοιο τέλοσδε (dichthadias kēras pheremen thanatoio telosde)
short: Thetis has told Achilles of two possible destinies: stay and die young with undying fame, or go home and live long without it.
body: A kēr is a doom of death, sometimes personified. Achilles says two such fates are carrying him 'to the end of death': if he fights at Troy, his homecoming (nostos) is lost but his fame will be imperishable; if he returns home, his fame is lost but his life will be long. Leaf observes that nowhere else in the poem is Achilles presented as having such a choice: in Book 1 he speaks as if a short life is simply fixed for him (1.352, 1.416), and Thetis in Book 18 confirms that his death follows soon after Hector's (18.95-6). Some analysts took this as a sign of different layers of tradition; others see a deliberate dramatisation, since the hero's choice is what gives his death meaning. Nagy reads the alternatives as kleos versus nostos, the themes of the Iliad and the Odyssey respectively. By Book 18 Achilles has chosen, knowingly, to stay and die.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.411
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.410-416
Homer, Iliad 18.94-6 (Thetis: Achilles' death follows Hector's)

title: Kleos aphthiton: imperishable fame
greek: κλέος ἄφθιτον ἔσται (kleos aphthiton estai)
short: The only Iliadic instance of 'imperishable fame', a phrase with an exact match in the Sanskrit Rig Veda; its status as inherited Indo-European poetry is debated.
body: Kleos, from the verb 'to hear', is what is said and sung about a person; aphthiton, 'unwilting, unperishing', is used elsewhere of divine objects. In 1967 Rüdiger Schmitt and in 1974 Gregory Nagy argued that kleos aphthiton is cognate with Vedic śrávas ákṣitam, 'imperishable fame', and so preserves a phrase of Indo-European poetry more than two thousand years older than Homer. Margalit Finkelberg (1986) objected that it occurs only once in Homer and does not behave like a fixed formula, so it may be a Greek coinage; E. D. Floyd argued that the Vedic expression meant something more material. Nagy adds a pun: aphthiton echoes Phthia, Achilles' homeland, so a homecoming to 'the land of wilting' is the life without undying fame. Either way the line names what the Iliad itself provides: Achilles' kleos survives because the song is still sung.

sources.cite: Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.413
Margalit Finkelberg, 'Is κλέος ἄφθιτον a Homeric formula?', Classical Quarterly 36 (1986) 1-5

title: Phoenix's quarrel with Amyntor and the lost lines
greek: ὡς μὴ πατροφόνος μετ' Ἀχαιοῖσιν καλεοίμην (hōs mē patrophonos met' Achaioisin kaleoimēn)
short: Phoenix confesses that he planned to kill his father; the four lines saying so (9.458-61) are missing from our manuscripts and survive only in a quotation by Plutarch.
body: Phoenix's life story mirrors Achilles' situation. At his mother's urging he slept with his father Amyntor's concubine; Amyntor cursed him with childlessness, and in anger Phoenix thought of killing his father, until a god reminded him of what people would say. He fled to Peleus, who made him a king and gave him Achilles to rear. The lines 9.458-61 ('then I planned to kill him with the sharp bronze...so that I should not be called a father-slayer among the Achaeans') are not in the medieval manuscripts. Plutarch quotes them in How the Young Man Should Study Poetry (Moralia 26F) and says that Aristarchus removed them out of fear, presumably because a hero contemplating parricide seemed shocking. Leaf argues that the lines are neither essential to the context nor un-Homeric, doubts that Aristarchus really removed them, and notes that they were first put into printed texts in 1707; Murray includes them. The passage shows Phoenix teaching Achilles that he too once let anger rule him and that public opinion restrained him: an example of anger mastered.

title: The Erinyes, avengers of curses
greek: Ἐρινῦς (Erinus); Ζεὺς καταχθόνιος (Zeus katachthonios); ἠεροφοῖτις (ēerophoitis)
short: Amyntor calls on the Erinyes to fulfil his curse; 'Zeus of the underworld' (Hades) and Persephone grant it. In the Meleager story an Erinys 'walking in mist' hears Althaea's curse.
body: The Erinyes (Latin Furies) are underworld powers who enforce the rights of parents, elders and the dead, above all by making curses effective. Hesiod makes them daughters of Earth, born from the blood of the castrated Ouranos (Theogony 185). In Phoenix's speech they appear twice, framing his story and the story of Meleager: Amyntor's curse makes Phoenix childless, which is why he raised Achilles as his son, and Althaea's curse brings death on Meleager. 'Zeus katachthonios', Murray's 'Zeus of the nether world', is a title of Hades, ruler below as Zeus is above. Leaf explains the epithet ēerophoitis at 9.571 as 'walking in darkness', found only here and at 19.87, where Agamemnon blames an Erinys for his atē. The Erinyes' later role in Aeschylus' Eumenides, pursuing Orestes for killing his mother, develops this Homeric idea of the curse of a wronged parent.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.571

title: The allegory of the Prayers (Litai) and Atē
greek: Λιταί εἰσι Διὸς κοῦραι μεγάλοιο, χωλαί τε ῥυσαί τε παραβλῶπές τ' ὀφθαλμώ (Litai ... Atē)
short: Phoenix turns apology into myth: the Prayers, lame, wrinkled and squinting, follow swift Atē (Ruin) to heal her harm; whoever spurns them is struck by Atē in turn.
body: This is one of the few fully developed allegories in Homer. Atē, the delusion that makes men sin, is strong and swift-footed and runs ahead over all the earth; the Litai, 'Prayers' or entreaties for pardon, limp after her, wrinkled and with eyes cast aside (in shame, or looking anxiously), trying to repair the damage. Leaf divides the passage into two parts: lines 502-7 describe the offender, surprised by atē and then repentant; lines 508-12 put the responsibility on the injured party. If he respects the Prayers they help him; if he refuses, they ask Zeus to send Atē upon him so that he 'pays the penalty'. Nagy states the consequence for Achilles: refusing compensation risks a new cycle of atē for the refuser. This is exactly what happens: Achilles' refusal leads to Patroclus' death, and in Book 19 Agamemnon tells the companion myth of Atē cast out of Olympus.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.502-512
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.502-512

title: The story of Meleager (paradeigma)
greek: Κουρῆτές τ' ἐμάχοντο καὶ Αἰτωλοὶ μενεχάρμαι (Kourētes ... Aitōloi); Μελέαγρος (Meleagros)
short: Phoenix's cautionary tale: Meleager, angry, refused to defend Calydon despite gifts and pleas, fought at last when the city burned, and lost the gifts. The parallel with Achilles is exact.
body: Oeneus of Calydon forgot Artemis at his harvest sacrifice, and she sent a monstrous boar; after it was killed, the Aetolians of Calydon and the Curetes fought over its head and hide. Meleager, angered by his mother Althaea's curse (in fuller versions because he had killed her brothers), withdrew to his wife's side. Elders, priests, his father, sisters, mother and dearest companions begged him in turn; only when the city was burning did his wife Cleopatra persuade him, and then he fought without receiving the promised gifts. Leaf reconstructs the fuller myth (compare Apollodorus 1.8.2-3) and notes that Homer tells it only partially. J. T. Kakridis showed the 'ascending scale of affection' in the list of suppliants; M. M. Willcock argued that Homer adapts myths freely to make them fit their purpose as examples (paradeigmata). The story's lesson, 'come while gifts may be had', is ironic: Achilles too will fight only when the ships burn, and for Patroclus' sake.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.529
J. T. Kakridis, Homeric Researches, Lund: Gleerup, 1949, ch. 1 (the Meleager story)
M. M. Willcock, 'Mythological Paradeigma in the Iliad', Classical Quarterly 14 (1964) 141-154

title: Cleopatra (Alcyone), Meleager's wife
greek: Κλεοπάτρη (Kleopatrē); Ἀλκυόνη (Alkuonē)
short: Meleager's wife, whose name reverses the elements of Patroclus' name (kleos + patēr), is the last and most effective suppliant; she was also called Alcyone after the halcyon.
body: Kleo-patrē, 'glory of the father', is formed from the same two elements as Patro-klos in the opposite order, and many scholars, Nagy among them, see the pairing as meaningful: in the Meleager story the hero yields only to his wife, at the top of the 'ascending scale of affection'; in the Iliad Achilles returns to battle only for Patroclus, his dearest companion. Phoenix's digression gives her ancestry: daughter of Marpessa, whom the mortal Idas fought Apollo to keep. Leaf summarises the myth from the scholia and Apollodorus (1.7.8-9) and notes that it was shown on the Chest of Cypselus (Pausanias 5.18.2). Her parents called her Alcyone because her mother wept like the halcyon, the kingfisher said in Greek lore to cry mournfully for its mate. Cleopatra's description of a captured city (9.591-4) is what finally moves Meleager, a reminder of the fate awaiting Troy.

sources.cite: Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.524-599 and I.09.561-564

title: Blood-price (poinē)
greek: καὶ μέν τίς τε κασιγνήτοιο φονῆος ποινὴν ἢ οὗ παιδὸς ἐδέξατο τεθνηῶτος
short: Ajax appeals to custom: men accept a blood-price even from a brother's or son's killer, yet Achilles refuses compensation for one girl.
body: Ajax, the bluntest of the envoys, speaks to Odysseus and about Achilles rather than to him, and his argument is legal. In early Greek society homicide could be settled by poinē, a payment by the killer to the victim's family, after which the killer could remain in the community and the kinsman's anger was 'checked'. The trial scene on the shield of Achilles shows exactly such a dispute over the blood-price for a dead man (18.497-508). Leaf discusses the text of 9.632-3 (whether 'killer' or 'killing' of his brother) and the construction 'blood-price for his son'. Ajax's point is that even the gravest injury has a customary remedy, while Achilles' heart has become 'savage' (agrion, 9.629) 'because of one girl', when he is offered seven. Achilles grants that Ajax speaks after his own mind, but cannot master his anger at Agamemnon's insult.

anchor: some alien that had no rights
title: A dishonoured migrant (atimētos metanastēs)
greek: ὡς εἴ τιν' ἀτίμητον μετανάστην (hōs ei tin' atimēton metanastēn)
short: Achilles says Agamemnon treated him like an atimētos metanastēs, a dishonoured incomer without status in the community; he repeats the line in Book 16.
body: Metanastēs means one who has moved from his home and settled elsewhere; atimētos, 'without timē', means without honour or legal standing. Leaf explains that in societies built on kin and clan the man who had to leave his home lost his protection and became contemptible, 'clanless, lawless, hearthless' (9.63); he compares the low status of the metic at Athens and notes that in many languages the word for an outcast has become a general word of contempt, as with English 'wretch'. The line is repeated at 16.59, where Achilles, sending Patroclus out to battle, still feels the same humiliation. The phrase reveals what the quarrel was about for Achilles: not the girl as such, but public treatment that placed the best of the Achaeans below the lowest member of the community.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 9.648

title: Achilles' three answers
greek: πρίν γ' υἱὸν Πριάμοιο δαΐφρονος, Ἕκτορα δῖον, Μυρμιδόνων ἐπί τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας ἱκέσθαι
short: Achilles' replies soften by stages: to Odysseus he will sail home; to Phoenix he will decide at dawn; to Ajax he will not fight until Hector fires the Myrmidons' ships.
body: Each envoy draws a different answer. To Odysseus, Achilles says he will launch his ships tomorrow and be in Phthia on the third day (9.356-63). To Phoenix he says they will decide at dawn whether to go home or stay (9.618-19), and his reply is far shorter than the first. To Ajax he says he will not think of bloody war until Hector reaches the huts and ships of the Myrmidons, killing Argives and firing the ships (9.650-5). Nagy notes how stark the last answer is, and how it fixes the condition under which the plot will move. The embassy fails in its purpose but changes the situation: Achilles no longer threatens to leave Troy, and the fire on the ships in Book 16 will be the moment he sends out Patroclus. Odysseus, reporting back, mentions only the first and harshest answer (9.677-92), leaving the council in despair until Diomedes rallies it.

sources.cite: Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.09.606-619 and I.09.650-653

anchor: steep Scyrus, the city of Enyeus
title: Scyros, sacked by Achilles
greek: Σκῦρον ἑλὼν αἰπεῖαν, Ἐνυῆος πτολίεθρον (Skuron helōn aipeian, Enuēos ptoliethron)
short: In Homer Achilles captured Scyros and gave Iphis from there to Patroclus; the later legend of Achilles hidden among girls on Scyros is not Homeric.
body: The book ends with each hero lying beside a captive woman: Achilles with Diomede, daughter of Phorbas, from Lesbos, and Patroclus with Iphis, whom Achilles gave him after taking Scyros, the island city of Enyeus. In Homer Scyros is therefore a place Achilles sacked. Later tradition told a different story: Thetis, knowing her son's fate, hid him at the court of king Lycomedes on Scyros disguised as a girl, where he fathered Neoptolemus, until Odysseus exposed him (Apollodorus 3.13.8; Statius, Achilleid). The Iliad knows that Neoptolemus is being reared on Scyros (19.326-7), but Leaf comments that the legend of Achilles' sojourn on Scyros is evidently not Homeric. The quiet final scene, with Briseis absent, also reminds the audience of what Achilles has lost.
